title: Neural+Symbolic Approaches for Interpretable Actor-Critic Reinforcement Learning
claim: Opaque black-box models force unreliable post-hoc explanations; ours makes decisions through transparent rules that directly explain each action.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, dashed borders, bottom-to-top flow, speech-bubble contrast
description: Two dashed-border panels compare classic and proposed actor-critic. On the left, "Blackbox Actor Critic" shows two dark 3D boxes, a Blackbox Critic below a Blackbox Actor, joined by a TD arrow. A "decide" arrow leads up to "Action". A purple human icon with a cloud thought bubble complains that the post-hoc explanation (y<10) makes no sense. On the right, "Interpretable Neural+Symbolic Actor Critic" keeps a dark Blackbox Critic but uses a white Whitebox Actor with a boxing-glove icon. The actor links by arrow to a sketchy "Rules" card listing actions with conditions such as x>100. The rules feed back to "Action". A blue human icon with a blue box says the action is reasonable. The dark and light boxes carry the contrast.
caption: Comparative illustration of Neural+Symbolic Actor-Critic (NSAC) and classic Actor-Critic methods.
abstract: The integration of neural networks into actor-critic frameworks has been pivotal in advancing the field of reinforcement learning, enabling agents to perform complex tasks with greater efficiency and adaptability. However, neural network-based actor-critic models remain opaque ``black boxes,'' concealing their decision-making processes and hindering their use in critical applications where transparent and explainable reasoning is essential. This work introduces an innovative adaptation of the actor-critic framework that unites neural networks with rule ensembles to tackle key challenges in reinforcement learning. We harness the computational power, scalability, and adaptability of neural networks to model the critic, while integrating a rule ensemble system for the actor, ensuring transparency and interpretability for decision-making. Our study establishes a theoretical foundation for integrating rule ensembles into the Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) framework. Experimental results from seven classic and complex environments demonstrate that our proposed method matches or exceeds the performance of representative RL models, including symbolic methods, while offering self-interpretability and transparency.
